title: O, Kinch, thou art in peril. Get thee a breechpad.
html_source:
We can identify that Buck is talking about Bloom as he dubs him “the wandering jew.” He then jokingly—but also maliciously— tells Stephen (Kinch) that he’s in trouble because Bloom looked at him in a manner that Buck perceives as lustful (he had previously suggested Bloom is gay). The word “breechpad” used in this context gives the reader the idea that he is telling Stephen to protect his body from Bloom’s homosexual desires: the word “breech” can be used to refer to a person’s buttocks. This ridiculous idea builds on the character of Buck, demonstrating his flippant personality and willingness to say anything.

Because this entire chapter is devoted to Stephen and his Shakespeare/Hamlet theory, it is also worth noting that the way Buck says “Get thee a breechpad,” is reminiscent of Hamlet saying to Ophelia “Get thee to a nunnery” (3.1.138-139), thus implying that Ophelia is sexually promiscuous. The two lines not only sound and read similar to one another but both also have sexual connotations.
